why: Evidence standards vs signs of AI-written work vs detector reliability.

options.name: Evidence standards for AI-misuse findings
options.covers: What evidence is needed, or not sufficient, to find AI misuse: a standard of proof, the kinds of evidence to weigh, or the statement that a hunch that work 'does not sound like the student' is not enough. Evidence: Cornell, Grinnell, Iowa State, Clark, Georgetown. Broadened 2026-10-26 (D33): also covers rules that detector output may be used only as supporting evidence, not as proof. Evidence: Oberlin, Rice, Santa Clara, Old Dominion, Rowan.

options.name: Signs and indicators of AI-written work
options.covers: Manual signs, comparisons and indicators instructors use to suspect AI-written work (style shifts, fabricated citations, comparison with earlier work), as distinct from detector tools (P40) and standards of proof (P69).

options.name: Reliability and use of AI detectors
options.covers: AI detectors are unreliable or will not be used or relied upon as proof.

units.passage: Faculty members should remain attentive to work that is technically inconsistent or unusual, that may signal inappropriate use of generative AI.
units.why: 'Faculty members should remain attentive to work that is technically inconsistent or unusual, that may signal inappropriate use' tells faculty to watch for a sign of misuse; it names no detector, log, evidence standard or procedure, so neither process evidence nor evidence standards fits, and it is UNCOVERED.

units.passage: The evaluation of an AI detection tool alone is not sufficient evidence to conclude thata student has violated any rules.
units.why: 'The evaluation of an AI detection tool alone is not sufficient evidence to conclude that a student has violated any rules' sets an evidence standard for misuse (P69), not just that detectors are unreliable (P39).

units.passage: Suspected use of Generative AI in coursework is not sufficient evidence to begin a formal Academic Integrity investigation.
units.why: "Suspected use ... is not sufficient evidence to begin a formal Academic Integrity investigation" sets an evidence standard, P69.

units.passage: Look for unusual consistency in tone or style, especially if it deviates from a student’s previous work. AI-generated text may also include overly generic or repetitive phrases, lack of deep analysis, or produce content that appears superficially polished but lacks the nuanced understanding expected from human authors.
units.why: The list of signs ('unusual consistency in tone or style', 'overly generic or repetitive phrases') names kinds of evidence to weigh when judging AI misuse, which is P69; it is not P40 because no tool is involved.

units.passage: However, it’s important to use these tools as part of a broader assessment rather than relying on them exclusively. Combine them with your own judgment and knowledge of your students’ work to make a well-informed decision.
units.policy: Detection tools are used as part of a broader assessment, not relied on exclusively, and combined with the instructor's judgment and knowledge of students' work.
units.why: 'use these tools as part of a broader assessment rather than relying on them exclusively' says detector output is supporting evidence only, matching the broadened P69 (not P39, which says detectors are unreliable or not used).

units.passage: It is important to note that any AI detection platform should not be used as a sole source of identifying academic dishonesty when considering AI use.
units.why: "any AI detection platform should not be used as a sole source of identifying academic dishonesty" is a direct rule against sole reliance, P39.

units.passage: Their use as evidence for academic dishonesty is STRONGLY DISCOURAGED by many national education organizations, and ACC policy forbids them from being used as the sole evidence of academic dishonesty
units.why: "ACC policy forbids them from being used as the sole evidence" bars reliance on detectors as proof (P39).

units.passage: Be sure to include any samples of earlier/baseline student writing to which the writing in question can be compared.
units.why: The memo tells instructors to 'include any samples of earlier/baseline student writing to which the writing in question can be compared' when reporting suspected misuse. That says what evidence supports an AI-misuse report, so P69 (evidence for misuse findings) fits; P40 (tools and logs used to identify misuse) fits less well because no tool or log is named. Instructor, when-misuse, should.

units.passage: Note: Before challenging students about the originality of their work, please review these links on what certain indicators mean, how false positives are handled, and some FAQs: AI Writing Detection Handling False Positives in AI: Educator's Guide AI Writing Detection Frequently Asked Questions Turnitin Draft Coach (for students) guides students in drafting assignments to properly cite references.

units.passage: These tools cannot reliably determine whether AI was used in the creation of a student’s work and should not be considered definitive evidence of academic misconduct.

units.passage: Instead, concerns about potential misuse of AI should be evaluated using academic judgment, course context, the nature of the assignment, and supporting evidence.

units.passage: In addition, it is important for instructors to note that when submitted as evidence in an incident report of suspected use of AI, a report from an AI detection tool confirming such use can not be used as the sole piece of proof in a Dean’s Discipline case to find a student responsible for a violation of policy

units.why: "AI detector output may prompt a conversation with a student but does not alone support a finding of misconduct" limits detector output to supporting evidence (P69; P39 is close).

units.passage: The University's existing standard of proof applies.
units.why: "The University's existing standard of proof applies" sets the evidence standard for AI findings (P69).
